title: The if-else statement: choose between two paths

visuals.title: if (n % 2 == 0): even or odd?

branches.label: TRUE: the if block runs and prints "n is even."

visuals.elseLabel: FALSE: the else block runs and prints "n is odd."

goal: After this you can write an if-else statement that runs one block when a condition is true and another block when it is false.
warmup: Exam result: IF your marks are 50 or more, you pass; OTHERWISE you fail. Login: IF the password is correct, the door opens; OTHERWISE it says wrong password. In both cases something happens, and exactly one of the two actions is chosen. Voting is the same: IF age is 18 or more you may vote, otherwise you must wait.
definition: An if-else statement chooses between two paths using one condition. If the condition is true, the if block runs. If it is false, the else block runs. Exactly one of the two blocks always runs, never both and never none.
howItWorks: Move the slider. The condition is checked once. True sends the program down the if path; false sends it down the else path. After the chosen block finishes, the program continues with the line after the whole if-else.

worked.problem: Read a number n. Print whether it is even or odd (input: 7). A number is even if the remainder after dividing by 2 is 0.
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read n/]
  B --> C{"n % 2 == 0?"}
  C -- True --> D[/Print even/]
  C -- False --> E[/Print odd/]
  D --> F([End])
  E --> F

sample.title: Even or odd

explanation.text: n % 2 is the remainder after dividing by 2. If it is 0, the number is even.
Runs only when the condition is true.
Runs only when the condition is false.

steps.note: 7 % 2 is 1, and 1 == 0 is false. So we go to else.
The else block runs and prints the message.
The program ends. The if block was skipped.

worked.problem: Read the marks. Print Pass if marks are 50 or more, otherwise print Fail (input: 45).
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read marks/]
  B --> C{marks >= 50?}
  C -- True --> D[/Print Pass/]
  C -- False --> E[/Print Fail/]
  D --> F([End])
  E --> F

sample.title: Pass or fail

explanation.text: Runs when the condition is true.
Runs when the condition is false. Here the else sits on the same line as the closing brace; this style is also correct.

steps.note: Is 45 >= 50? No: false. Jump to else.

worked.problem: Read a person's age. If it is 18 or more, print "You can vote.". Otherwise print "You cannot vote yet." and also print how many years remain until 18 (input: 16).
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read age/]
  B --> C{age >= 18?}
  C -- True --> D[/Print You can vote/]
  C -- False --> E[/Print You cannot vote yet/]
  E --> G[wait = 18 - age]
  G --> H[/Print wait/]
  D --> F([End])
  H --> F

sample.title: Voting age
sample.expectedOutput:
Enter age: You cannot vote yet.
Years to wait: 2

explanation.text: True when age is 18 or more.
The else block starts here: it has two statements, so braces are needed.

steps.note: Is 16 >= 18? No: false. Go to else.
First statement of the else block.

variations.when: One statement in each part; braces optional
Nothing to do when false: use a plain if

mistakes.error: 'else' without a previous 'if' (an extra ; ended the if)
'else' without a previous 'if' (else never has its own condition)
lvalue required as left operand of assignment
'else' without a previous 'if' (two statements need braces before else)

examTips: Exactly one of the two blocks runs. Say this in every theory answer.
else has no condition and no semicolon after it.
Use braces when a block has two or more statements.
Even number test: n % 2 == 0. Odd: the else part, or n % 2 != 0.
In the flowchart, the diamond has two exits (True and False) which join again at the end.
romanSummary: if-else do raaston mein se ek raasta chunta hai.
Condition true ho to if wala block chalta hai, false ho to else wala block.
Dono mein se hamesha sirf ek block chalta hai, kabhi dono nahi.
else ke sath condition ya semicolon nahi lagta; zyada statements ho to braces { } lagayen.

practice.prompt: In an if-else statement, how many of the two blocks run?
practice.hint: Think of pass or fail: can you do both?
practice.explanation: The condition is checked once and exactly one of the two blocks runs.

practice.hint: 8 % 2 is the remainder of 8 divided by 2.
practice.explanation: 8 % 2 is 0, so the condition is true and Even is printed.
10 > 10 is false, so the else part prints B. C is after the if-else, so it always prints.
else has no condition. It runs when the if condition is false.

practice.hint: You want to compare, not assign.
practice.explanation: == compares the remainder with 1. (Note: for negative numbers n % 2 can be -1, so n % 2 != 0 is safer.)

practice.hint: The else block has two statements.
practice.explanation: a > b is false, so the whole else block runs: Y then Z.

practice.prompt: Write a program that reads the price of a ticket and the money you have. Print "Buy" if money is enough, otherwise "Not enough".
practice.explanation: Equal money is enough, so >= is used. Else covers the not-enough case.

quiz.prompt: Which part of if-else runs when the condition is false?
quiz.hint: Pass or fail: what is the 'otherwise' part?
quiz.explanation: The else block is the false path.
else is followed directly by its statement or block.

quiz.prompt: int n = 9; if (n % 2 == 0) cout << "E"; else cout << "O"; prints:
quiz.explanation: 9 % 2 is 1, not 0, so the condition is false and the else part runs.

quiz.prompt: When must you use braces in an else block?
options: When it has two or more statements
Only when the if has braces
quiz.answer: When it has two or more statements
quiz.hint: Without braces, how many statements belong to else?
quiz.explanation: Without braces only the first statement after else belongs to it.
